issues.subcategory: Contradiction between text and tables for donation means
issues.description: The text incorrectly reports the means for the identifiable and statistical victim conditions, swapping them compared to the data presented in Table 7. The text claims statistical victims received more donations (M=2.54) than identifiable victims (M=2.24), but Table 7 shows identifiable victims received higher mean donations (~2.54) than statistical victims (~2.25).
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between abstract and results for perceived impact
issues.description: The abstract claims that participants had a lower rating of perceived impact when facing an identifiable victim compared to statistical victims. However, the post-hoc results in Table 14 show no significant difference between the identifiable and statistical victim conditions (p = 1.000). The only significant difference was between the statistical and joint conditions.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The original study measured actual behavior by giving participants $5 and allowing them to donate it. The replication uses a hypothetical scenario where participants indicate how much they *would* donate. Hypothetical donations often suffer from hypothetical bias (cheap talk) and do not measure the same construct as actual financial sacrifice, fundamentally altering the nature of the dependent variable.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: Confounding of implicit and explicit interventions
issues.description: By crossing the Study 1 design (explicit intervention) with the Study 3 design (implicit intervention via the joint condition), the authors created a 'Joint / Intervention' condition that receives both an explicit lesson on the bias and an implicit joint presentation. The theoretical meaning of this double-intervention cell is unclear, and including it in the omnibus ANOVA alters the interpretation of the main effects compared to the original studies.
issues.quote: To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition to allow the comparison of explicit and implicit manipulation with fewer confounds.

issues.subcategory: Uncorrected multiple comparisons for segregated feelings
issues.description: The authors conducted six separate 2x3 ANOVAs for the segregated feeling variables (Table 13) without applying any correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni, FDR) to the alpha level. This inflates the family-wise error rate, making the marginally significant finding for perceived impact (p = .045) highly likely to be a false positive.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.subcategory: Missing descriptive statistics for segregated feelings
issues.description: The manuscript reports ANOVA results for six segregated feeling variables (Table 13) and post-hoc tests for perceived impact (Table 14), but completely fails to report the descriptive statistics (means and standard deviations) for these variables across the conditions in any table. A few means are only mentioned in passing in the text.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.subcategory: Missing details on exclusion criteria and attention checks
issues.description: The manuscript states that participants with prior knowledge or who failed an attention check were excluded, but it does not report the number of excluded participants, the nature of the attention check, or when the prior knowledge question was asked. If asked after the intervention, excluding based on prior knowledge could introduce post-treatment selection bias.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: Missing measurement details for the extension variable
issues.description: The manuscript introduces 'perceived impact of donation' as a novel extension variable but provides no details on how it was operationalized or measured. There is no information on the number of items, the wording of the questions, or the scale used.
issues.quote: We aim to extend the replication study by considering the “perceived impact of donation” as one of the feeling variables indicated in Small et al. (2007)’s Study 1.

issues.description: The authors classify their study as a 'close to very close replication' despite changing the dependent variable from actual monetary donation to hypothetical donation. According to the Lebel et al. (2018) framework they cite, a change in DV operationalization makes it a conceptual replication.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a 'close to very close replication'.

issues.subcategory: Inappropriate comparison of main effects with different degrees of freedom
issues.description: In Table 9, the authors directly compare the main effect of identifiability from the original study (which had 2 levels, df=1) to the replication (which has 3 levels, df=2). Because the replication includes the joint condition in the omnibus test, the F-statistic and effect size represent a different hypothesis than the original 2x2 design. They should have tested the 2x2 subset to directly replicate the original main effect.

The authors state they combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling, but they do not specify how this aggregation is performed (e.g., mean, sum, factor score) nor do they report the internal consistency (e.g., Cronbach's alpha) of this aggregated measure.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: Missing target sample size from power analysis
issues.description: The manuscript mentions that a power analysis was conducted and is available in the supplementary materials, but it fails to report the actual required sample size determined by this analysis in the main text. It only reports the N=1000 used for the dummy dataset.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study.

issues.description: The data analysis plan states that post-hoc contrast tests and pairwise comparisons will only be conducted if the omnibus or interaction effects are significant. While common, making planned contrasts conditional on omnibus tests is often statistically unnecessary and can reduce power to detect specific hypothesized differences.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly misspells the name of a prominent author in the field (Paul Slovic) as 'Solvic' in the text, which undermines the professionalism and attention to detail of the manuscript.
issues.quote: Solvic (2010) claimed... Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks...
